analysis.one_liner: Requires internet providers and many websites to get your permission before using or sharing sensitive personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House committee in July 2021 and died there without a hearing or a vote before the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require broadband providers and many websites and apps to clearly tell users what they do with personal data, get express permission (opt-in) before using sensitive information like health records, financial data, browsing history, or precise location, and honor opt-outs for less sensitive data. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and providers could not force users to sign away privacy rights to get service. However, the bill would also override every state privacy law, including stricter ones like California's.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users, who would gain clear notice of privacy practices and control over whether their sensitive information can be used or shared, and broadband providers and web companies, which would get one uniform federal privacy standard in place of a patchwork of state laws.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users; also web companies seeking one standard

how_it_helps.text: Providers of broadband service and many websites and apps must give users clear, conspicuous notice of their privacy policies before a user signs up, and keep that notice persistently available and flag material changes in advance.

Providers must get express opt-in consent before using, disclosing, or allowing access to sensitive user information, which the bill defines to include financial data, health information, Social Security numbers, precise location, the content of communications, and web browsing history.
For non-sensitive information, users get opt-out rights, and providers must offer a simple, free mechanism to grant, deny, or withdraw consent at any time, with the choice taking effect promptly.
Providers may not condition service on a user agreeing to waive privacy rights, and violations are enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission as unfair or deceptive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Broadband providers, websites, and apps would bear the cost of building consent systems and changing practices, and the online advertising ecosystem would lose some access to user data; ironically, users in states with stronger privacy laws could also lose, because the bill overrides state law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Internet providers, web companies, and the ad industry

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts all state laws relating to the privacy of user information, which would wipe out stricter existing protections such as California's, replacing them with a single federal floor.

Only sensitive information gets opt-in protection; for everything else, providers can keep collecting and using data unless the user affirmatively objects, and experience with opt-out systems shows most people never do.
Enforcement runs solely through the Federal Trade Commission; the bill gives individuals no right to sue on their own behalf.
Broad exceptions let providers use and share user information without any consent when it is 'necessary' to providing the service or for billing and collection, a carve-out that can be read broadly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real, tangible protections for the most sensitive categories of data, including browsing history and precise location, and a clear rule against forced privacy waivers. But those gains are undercut by the opt-out default for most data, FTC-only enforcement, broad service-provision exceptions, and a preemption clause that would erase stronger state laws. A privacy bill that overrides tougher state rules and relies entirely on one federal agency is a weak bargain even for people who want more control over their data.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee the day after introduction, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Lisa McClain introduced the bill on July 22, 2021, joined by five Republican cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the next day to its Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
No further action was taken for the rest of the 117th Congress, which ended January 3, 2023, so the bill never reached the House floor and never got a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The online data and advertising industry is better off, since the status quo of collecting user data with minimal federal rules continued untouched. Users gained nothing new, though people in states with stronger privacy laws at least kept those laws, which the bill would have overridden.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online data brokers and advertisers, unchanged

for.name: Rep. Lisa McClain
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: Five House Republican cosponsors (Reps. Babin, Cawthorn, Grothman, Owens, Steube)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a subcommittee or full committee markup, leaving it without a hearing or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, no Democrats signed on, and the Democratic-led committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill's opt-in rule for browsing history would curtail a core input to targeted advertising, but the opt-out default for other data, the broad service exceptions, and FTC-only enforcement leave the collection model largely intact. Preemption of stricter state laws would lock in a single, weaker federal standard.

ISPs would face new consent requirements for sensitive data, but they also gain the preemption of state privacy laws and a uniform federal rule, and the bill keeps them under FTC rather than tougher utility-style regulation by overriding the common-carrier exception.

Covered as 'edge services', platforms would owe users notice and consent mechanisms, but many already operate similar systems, and preemption would relieve them of complying with a patchwork of state rules.
